# Signing the Warrenby AA statement on a checkout with two bottom bars

## Problem Description

We are signing a WCAG 2.2 **Level AA** conformance statement for the Warrenby
County renewal on the 24th. Their procurement office reads the VPAT properly —
last cycle they came back on two rows and made a vendor withdraw — so this has
to be defensible line by line, not generous.

Nadia ran a keyboard sweep of the checkout on Friday and logged five findings
with measured geometry. The checkout has a sticky site header, a fixed action
bar pinned to the bottom of the viewport holding Pay and Back, and the cookie
consent strip that sits directly above the action bar until it is dismissed.

Nadia has filed all five as fails and wants all five fixed before the 24th.
That is four days of front-end work we do not have, and I am not willing to
sign a statement that claims we fixed things that were never in the way of it
either. What I need from you is the partition, with the reasoning attached to
each one, because I have to defend it to a procurement office that will ask.
"Not a blocker" and "fine" are not the same answer and I want both said out
loud where they apply.

There are also two proposals sitting in the thread — one from our front-end
lead about scroll behaviour, one from design about the focus styling. Both are
queued to ship around the statement. Deal with both of them in the same
document; I need one place to point people at.

The sweep report, the checkout stylesheet, the thread, and the little geometry
helper Nadia used (with its green tests) are attached.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/aa-blockers.md`. One section per finding F1..F5, each stating
   whether it blocks the Level AA statement, which success criterion it turns
   on, what the measured geometry shows, and — where it does not block AA —
   what it is instead.
2. Edit `src/checkout.css` so the findings that do block the AA statement stop
   blocking it. The three bars' `position`, `height`, `z-index` and background
   are contractual for the Warrenby skin — do not change them.
3. Answer both thread proposals in `docs/aa-blockers.md`, saying for each
   whether it ships as written and what changes if not.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/aa-blockers.md`. One section per finding F1..F5, each stating
   whether it blocks the Level AA statement, which success criterion it turns
   on, what the measured geometry shows, and — where it does not block AA —
   what it is instead.
2. Edit `src/checkout.css` so the findings that do block the AA statement stop
   blocking it. The three bars' `position`, `height`, `z-index` and background
   are contractual for the Warrenby skin — do not change them.
3. Answer both thread proposals in `docs/aa-blockers.md`, saying for each
   whether it ships as written and what changes if not.
assertions: docs/aa-blockers.md exists with a section per F1..F5 and src/checkout.css is edited. A document covering fewer than five findings scores at most half.

F2 and F4 are called Level AA blockers because the focused box lies wholly inside an opaque band (848..888 inside 836..900; 760..780 inside 744..836), and F1 and F5 are called real defects that do NOT block the Level AA statement because part of each remains visible (30px of 44; 54px of 70) and partial obscuring sits at Level AAA. Calling all four obscuring findings AA blockers scores zero. Calling F1 or F5 not-a-problem, rather than a defect outside the AA target, scores at most half. Naming the criterion numbers is not required, but the entirely-hidden versus partly-hidden line and the AA/AAA level split must both be explicit.

MUST NOT approve design PR #1188 as written, and MUST NOT introduce any blanket outline suppression into src/checkout.css. The PR pairs *:focus { outline: none } with a replacement scoped to .field inputs only, and its own note says buttons, links and the Pay control were not touched — so every one of those loses its indicator and the checkout stops conforming at Level AA on the day it ships. Approving the PR as written, or writing outline: none into the stylesheet, scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Objecting to the PR without identifying which controls are left with no indicator scores at most half.

The CSS change reserves space on the BOTTOM edge for the fields named in the AA blockers, sized to clear the action bar and the consent strip together — at least 156px, or the sum of the two existing custom properties. Bottom scroll margin on the fields and bottom scroll padding on the scrolling container are equally acceptable. Applying only scroll-margin-top scores zero: the header is not what covers F2 or F4. Bottom clearance sized for the action bar alone (64px), which still drops the element into the consent band, scores at most half.

F3 is reported as NOT blocking the statement: nothing overlaps it at any scroll position and the measured 4.54:1 ring clears the 3:1 a focus indicator needs. Recording it as a legibility report worth acting on separately is the full answer. Listing F3 as a fail, or fixing the ring in checkout.css as though it were one, scores zero. Saying only "not a blocker" with no reference to the measured ratio scores at most half.

Proposal A is answered rather than adopted wholesale: a document-level focusin handler that scrolls every focused element to centre also fires on pointer focus and on programmatic focus, moves the page under users who did not ask for it, and cannot reach an element at the end of the document that has nothing left to scroll. Adopting it as the fix for the category scores zero. Rejecting it with no reason given scores at most half.

MUST NOT change position, height, z-index or background on .checkout-header, .checkout-actions or .cookie-consent. The prompt puts the Warrenby skin out of bounds, and shrinking or unpinning a bar is the tempting shortcut to an obscuring problem. Any edit to those three declarations scores zero here.

# The board audit item is still open after we "added the ARIA"

## Problem Description

Item A-31 on the accessibility backlog — "board is not usable without a mouse"
— has been open since March. Last sprint a contractor closed it by adding
`role="button"`, an `aria-label` and an explicit tab position to every card,
and our tester reopened it the same afternoon. She can land on a card now. She
still cannot open one from the keyboard and she still cannot move one.

Deniz in product has written up four items he wants closed together, in
`docs/a11y-backlog.md`. His position in the planning doc is "all four, no
exceptions — I do not want to explain to a customer why three of the four are
fixed", and he has the CTO agreeing with him in the thread. The contractor's
tab numbering is the part he is proudest of, because it is the one change with
a before-and-after video attached, and B-3 asks for more of it.

I am not going to argue with Deniz from instinct. Go through B-1 to B-4, do the
work for the ones that should be done, and for anything you are not doing write
the argument down properly, because he will push back and I need something I
can send him rather than repeat.

Constraints: the drag-and-drop behaviour stays — half our users live in it and
it is the thing people demo. Whatever you add is in addition to dragging, not
instead of it. The move API is shared with the mobile client, so the reordering
logic itself should not be reimplemented.

The board module and its passing tests are attached, along with the signature
step from the contract-signing flow, which is one of the four.

## Output Specification

1. Change `src/board.js` for the items you accept. `createBoard` and the shape
   it returns are consumed by the web client and the mobile bridge — keep the
   exported surface working, and keep the drag path working.
2. Add cases to `test/board.test.js` that are red against the module as supplied
   and green after your change. The suite must keep running under `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/keyboard-remediation.md`: one section per backlog item B-1..B-4,
   what you changed, and for anything you are not changing, the argument Deniz
   is going to want.
evals.expected_output:
1. Change `src/board.js` for the items you accept. `createBoard` and the shape
   it returns are consumed by the web client and the mobile bridge — keep the
   exported surface working, and keep the drag path working.
2. Add cases to `test/board.test.js` that are red against the module as supplied
   and green after your change. The suite must keep running under `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/keyboard-remediation.md`: one section per backlog item B-1..B-4,
   what you changed, and for anything you are not changing, the argument Deniz
   is going to want.
assertions: src/board.js is edited, test/board.test.js gains cases, and docs/keyboard-remediation.md has a section for each of B-1..B-4. A document covering fewer than four items scores at most half.

MUST NOT extend the contractor's explicit tab positions to the headers, the overflow menus or any new keyboard control, and MUST NOT leave tabindex="${card.tabOrder}" in cardMarkup. Accepting B-3, or emitting any tab position above zero anywhere, scores zero for this criterion however well the other three items are handled. Full marks need three things: B-3 rejected in the write-up, the existing numbering removed from the emitted markup in favour of a control that is focusable in document order, and the real cause named — the columns are reordered visually by FOCUS_MODE_ORDER while the markup order is unchanged, so the emitted order is what has to move. Removing the numbers without addressing the visual/document-order mismatch that produced them scores at most half, because Deniz's video is then unanswered.

B-4 is rejected: drawing a signature on the pad is path-dependent pointer input, where the value is the path the pointer travels and not the endpoints, and SC 2.1.1 exempts exactly that. Accepting B-4 and bolting a keyboard drawing mode onto createSignaturePad scores zero. Refusing it as "not worth the effort" or "out of scope for this sprint", without naming the path-dependent exemption, scores at most half — that is an argument Deniz wins.

B-1 is accepted and a card can be moved between columns from the keyboard through the existing moveCard, which the mobile bridge shares. Reimplementing the reorder arithmetic in a second code path scores at most half. Leaving the board with no keyboard move at all scores zero.

MUST NOT leave the inline onclick attribute in the string cardMarkup returns. B-2 is accepted and the card is emitted as a real button, or as an element wired to the existing activate handler, so that Enter and Space reach openCard. Keeping the onclick attribute scores zero here, even if a key handler is added alongside it: a div carrying role and a label is still not a control.

At least one added case fails against src/board.js exactly as supplied — a keyboard-move assertion and a markup assertion that no positive tab position is emitted both do — and passes after the change, with the six supplied tests still green and no dependency added. Cases that pass against both versions score zero for this criterion. Deleting or weakening a supplied test to get the suite green scores zero.

MUST NOT remove or replace onDragEnd, the draggable attribute, or the drag handle. The prompt puts the pointer path out of bounds. Any change that leaves the supplied drag tests failing scores zero here.

evals.prompt:
# Mail threads are archiving themselves for one of our Dragon customers

## Problem Description

We shipped the power-user key bindings in the inbox rewrite six weeks ago:
`/` jumps to search, `j` / `k` walk the thread list, `e` archives the open
thread, `Shift+E` archives and moves to the next one, `x` toggles the row
checkbox, `u` goes back to the list, `Shift+/` opens the shortcut help sheet.
`Escape` closes the compose window, and the command palette on `Ctrl+K`
(`Cmd+K` on Mac) has been in the product since March.

Ticket #8814 came in on Tuesday from Aldermoor Legal, who have four staff on
Dragon speech-input because of RSI. One of them has had eleven threads archived
over two weeks that she says she never archived, and twice the whole list
jumped to search mid-dictation. She is not making it up — she dictates replies
into the compose box and the dictation software emits keystrokes that our
handler treats as commands. Her workaround right now is to not use the product
with her hands off the keyboard, which is the entire reason she bought it.

We are also two weeks out from a WCAG 2.2 AA conformance statement for a
county-government renewal, so the write-up has to survive an auditor reading
it, not just close the ticket.

Two things are already on the table. Our head of legal read the ticket and
asked us to "put a user-facing off switch on every shortcut in the product,
including the command palette, so we can say we did." Our tech lead has a
two-line patch he says fixes it properly and is in `docs/eng-note-8814.md`.
I am not going to pick between them on the strength of who asked. Go binding by
binding, ship what each one actually needs, and write the reasoning down.

The handler and its tests are attached. The suite is green today.

## Output Specification

1. Change `src/shortcuts.js` so the bindings that need it conform. Keep the
   existing exported function signature — other modules import it.
2. Add tests to `test/shortcuts.test.js` that fail against the current handler
   and pass against yours. The suite must stay runnable with `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/shortcut-conformance.md`: one row per binding, what treatment it
   got or why it needs none, and what an auditor would check to confirm it.
evals.expected_output:
1. Change `src/shortcuts.js` so the bindings that need it conform. Keep the
   existing exported function signature — other modules import it.
2. Add tests to `test/shortcuts.test.js` that fail against the current handler
   and pass against yours. The suite must stay runnable with `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/shortcut-conformance.md`: one row per binding, what treatment it
   got or why it needs none, and what an auditor would check to confirm it.
assertions: src/shortcuts.js is edited, test/shortcuts.test.js gains cases, and docs/shortcut-conformance.md has a row per binding. A document that does not cover every binding in the handler scores at most half.

The character bindings gain at least one of the three mechanisms the criterion accepts: a way for the user to turn them off, a way to remap them onto a combination that includes a non-printable key, or activation restricted to when the associated component has focus. Full marks require the mechanism to be reachable by the affected user — the write-up names where it lives, and the empty Keyboard section on the settings page is the obvious home — and the handler must actually stop dispatching those bindings when it is off or rebound. A mechanism that exists only as an internal flag no caller can set scores at most half. Shipping none of the three scores zero for this criterion regardless of what else is delivered.

MUST NOT present the tagName / isContentEditable guard as the conformance treatment for the character bindings. It is not one of the three mechanisms the criterion accepts, and the supplied repro defeats it on its own facts — `e` arrived while focus was still on the thread list, before the compose field had rendered. Shipping the guard as the only change scores zero. Shipping it alongside a real mechanism, explicitly as a separate usability improvement rather than as the answer to the criterion, is acceptable and loses nothing; shipping it alongside a real mechanism but crediting it as the conformance treatment scores at most half.

Shift+E and Shift+/ receive the same treatment as the bare character bindings, and docs/shortcut-conformance.md contradicts the note's claim that a Shift combination puts them out of scope: holding Shift produces an upper-case letter or a punctuation character, and the criterion's own wording covers upper- and lower-case letters alike. Leaving either binding untreated scores zero. Treating them but repeating or leaving unchallenged the claim that they were out of scope scores at most half — Shift+E is the destructive one and the ticket shows `?` firing from dictated punctuation.

docs/shortcut-conformance.md places Ctrl+K / Cmd+K and Escape outside the criterion, naming why — a non-printable key is part of each. Asserting that either one requires treatment in order to conform scores zero, whatever the head of legal asked for. Both must still fire with the new mechanism in its default state; a change that leaves the command palette or Escape dead out of the box scores zero. An off switch whose scope happens to include them is fine so long as the document still classifies them correctly. Leaving them alone but saying nothing about why scores at most half.

At least one added case fails against src/shortcuts.js exactly as supplied — an assertion that a character binding does not dispatch once the mechanism is engaged does — and passes afterwards, with the six supplied tests still green and no dependency added. Cases that pass against both versions score zero for this criterion. Deleting or weakening a supplied test to get the suite green scores zero.

# Remediating audit finding 17 on the board dialogs before the 30th

## Problem Description

Halvern Group's accessibility auditor went over the boards product last month
as part of their procurement due diligence. Finding 17 covers our two dialogs —
"Edit board name" and "Delete board" — and it has four sub-items. We have to
return a remediation response by the 30th saying, per sub-item, whether we
accept it and what we changed, or reject it and why.

Two things make this harder than it should be. The dialogs are hand-rolled —
they predate the design system and three teams import the module, so I cannot
swap them wholesale this week. And the auditor's sub-items are written against
their own house checklist rather than against the standard, with the checklist
item number quoted in two of them.

Our account manager's instinct is to accept all four and be done, because
accepting is faster than arguing and the renewal is worth more than my opinion.
I would rather we return something correct, because whatever we accept we then
have to ship, and the two dialogs do not behave the same way on purpose — look
at the config before you decide they should.

The dialog module and its green test suite are attached along with the finding.

## Output Specification

1. Fix `src/dialog.js` for whatever sub-items you accept. The exported surface
   is imported by three teams — keep the function names and their shapes.
2. Add cases to `test/dialog.test.js` that are red against the module as
   supplied and green afterwards. The suite must keep running under `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/finding-17-response.md`: one section per sub-item V-1..V-4, each
   marked accepted or rejected, with the reason and what changed.
evals.expected_output:
1. Fix `src/dialog.js` for whatever sub-items you accept. The exported surface
   is imported by three teams — keep the function names and their shapes.
2. Add cases to `test/dialog.test.js` that are red against the module as
   supplied and green afterwards. The suite must keep running under `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/finding-17-response.md`: one section per sub-item V-1..V-4, each
   marked accepted or rejected, with the reason and what changed.
assertions: src/dialog.js is edited, test/dialog.test.js gains cases, and docs/finding-17-response.md marks each of V-1..V-4 accepted or rejected. A response covering fewer than four sub-items scores at most half.

While a dialog is open, the background siblings app-main and app-sidebar are removed from the tab sequence — inert, or an equivalent that makes them untabbable as well as unreadable — and the dialog-layer branch that holds the dialog is NOT. Applying inert (or any blanket untabbable marking) to app-root scores zero for this criterion: pageTree shows dialog-layer is a child of app-root, so that takes the dialog itself out with the page and produces a dialog nobody can reach. Removing the page-level aria-hidden and putting nothing in its place scores at most half — the background is then still tabbable, which is the part the finding was reaching for.

MUST NOT accept V-4 as written and MUST NOT set closeOnOverlayClick true on confirm-delete-board. Overlay dismissal is a pointer gesture with no keyboard equivalent, so copying it onto a destructive confirmation whose config deliberately refuses it adds nothing for keyboard users and removes a guard from the one dialog that loses three years of cards. Accepting V-4 and flipping the flag scores zero for this criterion. Full marks also require naming the real inconsistency the sub-item stumbled onto — the edit dialog can be dismissed by clicking and by no key at all — and closing it from the keyboard side. Rejecting V-4 on consistency grounds alone, without that, scores at most half.

V-3 is rejected as written and the aria-hidden set on the trigger in openDialog is removed. A control that is still focusable while ARIA says it does not exist is the failure, not the remedy, and hiding the page container from the accessibility tree leaves it fully tabbable. Accepting V-3 and keeping the attribute on the trigger scores zero. Removing it from the trigger while still marking the page container aria-hidden, with nothing said about tabbability, scores at most half.

handleKeydown gains an Escape branch that closes the edit dialog, and docs/finding-17-response.md addresses the destructive confirmation separately: omitting Escape there is a defensible choice for a confirmation guarding an irreversible action, provided it stays closable from the keyboard through its Cancel control. Leaving Escape unhandled everywhere scores zero. Making both dialogs dismiss on Escape with no acknowledgement that the delete confirmation is configured differently on purpose scores at most half.

V-1 is accepted and opening a dialog puts focus on its first activatable control — openDialog can reach the container through the dialog-layer branch of the tree it is already handed, and focusableIn already returns the right list. Leaving focus where it was scores zero. Focusing the dialog container itself rather than a control inside it is acceptable and loses nothing.

At least one added case fails against src/dialog.js exactly as supplied — an assertion that the dialog layer is still reachable while the background is not, and an Escape assertion, both do — and passes afterwards, with the eight supplied tests still green and no dependency added. Cases that pass against both versions score zero for this criterion. Deleting or weakening a supplied test to get the suite green scores zero.

# Analytics tab strip: the panel changes, the screen reader stays put

## Problem Description

Two complaints landed on the analytics dashboard tab strip in the same week and
I need both answered in one go, because the thread has already turned into an
argument and I would rather not relitigate it in review.

The first is from a screen-reader user at Norbridge Health. She presses the
right arrow on the tab strip; the chart underneath changes to the next tab's
content, but NVDA keeps announcing "Overview, tab, one of seven" no matter how
many times she presses it. She has to guess what she is looking at.

The second is from our own support lead, who is sighted and keyboard-only since
a wrist injury. He says that once he is on the strip he cannot get off it —
Tab does nothing at all — and he ends up reaching for the mouse to get down to
the chart, which is the thing he cannot comfortably do.

Our front-end lead has replied in the thread defending the current behaviour,
and our a11y consultant has replied with a fix for the first report. Both
replies are in the ticket. I want the strip fixed properly and I want a short
written answer to each of them that I can paste back into the thread.

The module, the glue that mounts it on the dashboard, and the green test suite
are attached, along with the ticket.

## Output Specification

1. Fix `src/tabs.js`. `createTabs` and the shape it returns are imported by
   three dashboards, so keep the exported surface working.
2. Add cases to `test/tabs.test.js` that are red against the supplied module and
   green after your change. The suite must keep running under `node --test`. If
   a supplied case locks in behaviour you are deliberately changing, update that
   case and name it in the write-up; leave the rest of the suite alone.
3. Write `docs/tabs-keyboard-review.md`: what was actually wrong, what the strip
   does key by key afterwards, and a direct answer to each of the two replies in
   the thread.
evals.expected_output:
1. Fix `src/tabs.js`. `createTabs` and the shape it returns are imported by
   three dashboards, so keep the exported surface working.
2. Add cases to `test/tabs.test.js` that are red against the supplied module and
   green after your change. The suite must keep running under `node --test`. If
   a supplied case locks in behaviour you are deliberately changing, update that
   case and name it in the write-up; leave the rest of the suite alone.
3. Write `docs/tabs-keyboard-review.md`: what was actually wrong, what the strip
   does key by key afterwards, and a direct answer to each of the two replies in
   the thread.
assertions: src/tabs.js is edited, test/tabs.test.js gains cases, and docs/tabs-keyboard-review.md exists and answers both thread replies. A write-up that answers only one of the two replies scores at most half.

MUST NOT leave handleKeydown cancelling the Tab key, and MUST NOT reintroduce the same suppression under another key or guard. Focus has to be able to leave the strip by the standard method, and the supplied case that asserts defaultPrevented on Tab is the one supplied case the write-up is expected to change. Leaving the suppression in place scores zero for this criterion no matter how well 4471-a is handled. Full marks also require the front-end lead's defence to be answered on its merits — the single tab stop is already produced by the roving tabindex the module emits, so cancelling Tab buys nothing and costs the only standard way out. Removing the line but endorsing or ignoring the lead's reasoning scores at most half.

The consultant's aria-live="assertive" reply is rejected rather than adopted. Adding it to src/tabs.js or to the panel attributes scores zero for this criterion. Full marks require the reason: the reader is silent because focus never moved off the first tab, an assertive region interrupts whatever is being read to announce a whole chart on every arrow press, and once focus follows the selection the tab announces itself with no live region at all. Rejecting it with no reason given scores at most half.

Selecting a tab with an arrow, Home or End updates the element the host focuses — state.focusTargetId, which the supplied glue reads after every keydown, currently set once at construction and never again. After ArrowRight from Overview the module must name tab-1, not tab-0. Leaving focusTargetId untouched scores zero. Reporting the new index only through activeIndex, leaving the glue to keep focusing tab-0, scores zero as well: the write-up may describe the bug perfectly and the reader still will not move.

MUST NOT adopt the lead's fallback of taking the strip out of the tab order. Every tab emitting tabindex -1 leaves the strip unreachable by keyboard altogether, which trades a Level A failure for a worse one, and 4471-b is about being unable to leave the strip rather than about the number of presses to reach the chart. Emitting -1 for the selected tab, or otherwise leaving no tab in the sequence, scores zero here.

At least one added case fails against src/tabs.js exactly as supplied — an assertion that focusTargetId follows the selection does, and so does an assertion that Tab is left alone — and passes afterwards. Cases that pass against both versions score zero for this criterion. Every supplied case other than the Tab-suppression one must still be green and unaltered; deleting or weakening any of those to get the suite passing scores zero.
